question_text: In a △ABC, show that cosA/a + cosB/b + cosC/c = (a² + b² + c²)/(2abc).

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — name each standard result you use and the order you use them in.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Substitute the cosine rule
steps.margin_note: Half the marks. Each cosine goes in as the cosine rule, and the 1/a outside multiplies the 1/(2bc) inside — giving 1/(2abc) every time.
steps.memory_tip: The 1/a outside multiplies the 1/(2bc) inside, giving 1/(2abc) every time.

recall.must_convey: That the cosine rule is substituted for each cosine and every denominator becomes 2abc.
accept: substitute the cosine rule for each and the denominators all become two a b c
one over a times one over two b c gives one over two a b c
every term ends up over two a b c
cosine rule substitute cheste anni two abc meeda vasthai
all three denominators are the same

steps.why: a × 2bc = 2abc whichever term you take, so all three land on the same denominator without any extra work.
common_mistakes: Getting different denominators and trying to find an LCM.

steps.label: Add and conclude
steps.margin_note: The other half. The three numerators cancel in pairs — each squared term survives once.
steps.memory_tip: Over the common denominator each squared term survives exactly once.

recall.must_convey: That the numerators add to a² + b² + c², giving (a²+b²+c²)/(2abc).
accept: add the numerators to get the sum of the squares over two a b c
each square survives once as before
the answer is a squared plus b squared plus c squared over two a b c
sum of squares by two abc vasthundi
the numerators give the sum of the squares

steps.why: The numerator collects to a² + b² + c², the same numerator as the 4Δ version of this identity; only the denominator differs, 2abc here. Noticing that saves re-deriving it.

insider_note: Substitute the cosine rule into each term and every denominator becomes 2abc. The three brackets then cancel in pairs, leaving only a² + b² + c² on top.
